question: An email from "IT Support" shows the address it-support@cloudly-helpdesk.example, but your company uses cloudly.example. What is the best action?
options: Reply and ask if it is real
Do not click anything; report it to your security team
Click the link to check where it goes
Forward it to coworkers as a warning
explanation: The domain differs from the organisation's real domain, a common spoofing sign. Reporting it lets security investigate.
incorrect: Replying, clicking or forwarding keeps you interacting with a likely malicious message. Report it through the official channel instead.

question: Which URL is most likely a typosquatting attempt of cloudly.example?
options: https://www.cloudly.example/login
https://accounts.cloudly.example/
https://cloud1y.example/login
https://cloudly.example/help
explanation: cloud1y.example swaps the letter l for the digit 1. The other URLs use the genuine domain or its subdomains.
incorrect: The other options use the real domain or a subdomain of it. Look for swapped, added or missing characters.

question: A message says your account will be deleted in 30 minutes unless you verify now. Which tactic is this?
options: Curiosity
Urgency and fear
Trust and familiarity
Reciprocity
explanation: Artificial deadlines and threats pressure people to act before thinking.
incorrect: The key clue is a short deadline combined with a threat of loss: urgency and fear.

question: You receive an unexpected invoice named invoice_2291.pdf.exe. What should you do?
options: Open it; PDFs are safe
Open it in a private window
Do not open it; the .exe extension means it is a program
Rename it to .pdf and open it
explanation: A double extension hides an executable. Verify unexpected attachments with the sender through a separate channel.
incorrect: The final extension (.exe) decides what the file is. Renaming or private windows do not make it safe.

question: A login page shows a padlock and the address https://northbridge-secure-login.example. The real bank is northbridge.example. Is the page safe?
options: Yes, the padlock proves it is legitimate
Yes, if the page looks identical
No, a padlock only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is genuine
Only if it asks for MFA
explanation: Attackers can obtain HTTPS certificates for their own domains. Always check the domain itself.
incorrect: HTTPS shows encryption, not trustworthiness, and copied designs are easy to build. The domain is what matters.

question: After you enter your password on a suspicious site, it asks you to type the MFA code you just received. What is likely happening?
options: Normal security verification
The attacker is relaying your code to log in as you
Your phone is out of sync
The site is upgrading security
explanation: Attackers can forward one-time codes to the real site in real time. Phishing-resistant MFA such as passkeys or security keys helps.
incorrect: A page reached from a message link that collects your code is a code-relay attack, not routine verification.

question: You entered your password on a fake page. What should you do first?
options: Wait to see if anything happens
Change the password on the real site from a trusted device and report it
Delete the email and forget it
Reply to the sender to complain
explanation: Act quickly: change the password (and any reuse), enable MFA, review account activity and tell IT/security.
incorrect: Delay or silence gives attackers time. Change credentials via the official site or app and report the incident.

question: You get an SMS: "Parcelo: delivery failed, pay a 1.99 fee at parcelo-track.example". You expect no parcel. Best response?
options: Pay the small fee
Reply STOP
Ignore the link and check the official Parcelo app or website typed manually
Click to see what it is
explanation: Small fees are used to capture card details. Go to the official service directly.
incorrect: Clicking or replying can confirm your number is active. Verify through a trusted channel.

question: The CEO emails finance from a personal address demanding an urgent, confidential gift card purchase. This is most likely:
options: Business email compromise / whaling-style impersonation
A normal request
A software bug
A newsletter
explanation: Executive impersonation with secrecy and speed is a classic warning sign. Verify via a known phone number or channel.
incorrect: Unusual payment requests with secrecy and urgency must be verified out-of-band.

question: A caller claims to be your bank and asks for your full card number and PIN to stop fraud. What do you do?
options: Provide the details to protect your account
End the call and phone the number on the back of your card
Give only the PIN
Ask them to email you
explanation: Banks do not ask for your PIN by phone. Hang up and call a number you already trust.
incorrect: Never give credentials to an inbound caller; call back on an independently sourced number.
